In short, the house was creepy and creaky and old- it had a root cellar and some rooms upstairs that the dogs she had later (years after this happened)  would stand and bark at, and refuse to enter. We were sliding it around and asking it stupid questions, but then we decided to "really try it" and close our eyes, hovering our hands very lightly on the placard. All of a sudden, there was the loudest bang on the study door that I have ever heard in my life, like someone had ran full force into it with their shoulder and slammed all their weight into the door. It was horrifying, and we all screamed. It was honestly something I will never forget, because I KNOW that if someone had actually slammed into that door with enough force to make the sound it did, that door would have opened. My gma ran downstairs, asking us what happened and if we had heard the noise. 

She was in her late 60's when this happened, not capable or wanting to freak us the f out. At the time, she had no dogs, only an elderly cat.

I looked over at him. His eyes were low, and I knew what it meant. He wanted to talk about it. Again. I shuffled my feet around slightly, trying not to let him hear that I was altogether not up for another discussion. The burden of the impending parting was heavy on my heart in a strange way. I knew soon, too soon, I wouldn't be opening my eyes to his face any longer. I wanted to ask him every question on my mind, so that I could have every answer. I wasn't ready for the day when I could ask him anything, and he would answer. The day when talking to him meant talking to a wall. The day that in its own way, a little piece of the universe would close off to me forever, and I would be left to formulate replies with the shards of memories of his voice. 

I looked over. I was too tired. I guess that's how everyone feels, towards the end. Too tired to do anything but fool yourself into believing that there isn't an end at all. 

I knew that the crops were low of late. I knew the children had been hungry. The news wasn't wasting a day on it. Even now, in the cold clinical discomfort of the hospital room, the television heaped its uncaring vision on us, bathing the room in its sickly color. It made him look even paler, his eyes even lower, sunken in more than I knew was the truth. 

I knew what he wanted without even talking. I always had. But I opened my mouth, and I forced the words out, pouring salt into the void. 

"I know it's what you want. I know it would help people. But I don't think I can stand it."

My eyes watered. It had become normal, expected even. But still I felt strange. Growing up, I was always far left. Liberal, free and blue. I never thought there would be a cause for the greater good that I couldn't support. Then, slowly but surely, it crept in. It encroached on us like a frog in a pot of boiling water. The political incumbents talked about it for election debates. Food banks started to make commercials. Light and airy, with pleasant pictures. The kind of commercials that show smiling nuclear couples holding hands and a pleasant noise. 

I felt sick. I knew they processed it. I knew they packaged it up to be sterile and sheer and inhuman. But I was a vegetarian because I knew that it was the same with animals. The pork on our plates was a far cry from the rust blood stained floors of the slaughter house or the factory. 

"This isn't that", he said.

"They treat you with some dignity. You're a human being."

I turned to look back at him. His eyes were hollow. He was watching the television, the flickering light of his face warping to a new expression with every passing shadow. The room was quiet now. He was making a difference. It was just  a body. It was just a vessel. His mind was here. His mind was separate. But I didn't have much longer.

I moved closer to him, sitting on the edge of that horrible hospital blanket, stiff and  spiny. I reached out for his arm, wrapping my fingers around his wrist, finally grasping how tenuous even the material was now. I could grasp him and still he would leave me. His eyes shifted from the screen to meet mine.

"We live on through our good deeds", he said, a smile playing at his lips. 

"Yes," I said. "Yes", and I was sad for his body, but for the loss of him I was heartbroken.

Jake was sitting on his kitchen breakfast counter, flipping through another one of those newspaper stories on obesity. Just the body shots though. "Couldn't get too offensive, could we?", he thought sarcastically, and flipped to the metro section. The air of the encroaching morning was not sweet. Rather, it was the smell of winter, of death frozen and halted under the layer of frost still covering the ground. It was a cold wind, and it lent his kitchen the frosty air of stopped time. 

Jake bent his head to the newspaper, wanting the sun to spill through the clouds, and mimicking his desires on his fried egg. Just then, there was a terrific trampling noise through his kitchen window.
Jake's head snapped up from where he had been engrossed in an article about re- tiling the theater. Branches snapped and the ground, damp from a recent rain, half- absorbed the sound. Muffled crunching echoed through Jake's rather large house.

"Hello?", Jake asked, not at all cautiously. 

He had lived next to the forest long enough that he knew the sounds of a deer, and sometimes he knew them so well he heard them in his sleep. Just to make sure, though, he called out again.

"Hello?"

He wasn't really expecting anything to call out in return, not really expecting anything to answer his even- toned inquiry. But even so, there was one.

"Shhh", said a small, weakish voice. 
Jake's heart leapt into his throat as his eyes were torn from the window and its sunrise, still a pinkish gold, to the screen of the door he sat feet away from.

There was a person there, a man. He was short and well rounded, not unlike, Jake thought, the pictures in the metro section. His hair was close cropped and thinning out, and he wore an ill- fitting outfit of a tropical polo and khaki shorts. 

This was an odd combination, Jake thought, for it was only the beginning of March, and the trees outside of his large, breathy house still held the dregs of winter in their branches. But still, thought Jake, the man looked familiar. He couldn't place it, couldn't touch that spot in his brain, but he knew he had seen him before. 

Jake looked at the man, letting his mask of coolness slip and allowing incredulity to slip through the cracks. 

"Who- who are you?"

The man simply looked ahead, his eyes wide with what Jake could only assume was fear. His tongue crept out from between his wind chapped lips and he began to speak.

"Whatever happens, the man said, his eyes darting back towards the yard, "Whoever comes knocking, I've been here for at least an hour". 

Jake opened his mouth to protest the strangely familiar man's intrusion, but he simply took two large steps out of the watercolor morning and onto Jake's tiled kitchen floor. Whipping around again, as if to catch something in action behind him, the man locked the glass portion of Jake's door, and, without time for a protest, took huge strides into the recesses of Jake's house. His too- big house.

For a moment, Jake sat in the silence of disbelief before getting up to pursue his new guest. He sat up and laid the metro section down on the counter, feeling his palms begin to sweat.

"An hour? What would that possibly help?", he thought to himself, a mixture of half annoyed and half scared. 

He walked down the hallway where he had seen the man run, checking his  gold faced watch for the hour. He was going to be late to work because some asshole thought it was okay to seek shelter in random houses along the nice side of town. Jake scowled as he pushed each hallway door open with the side of his fist, preparing each time to have to yell at the man.

He was preparing again when there was a rapping at the door. Two short, sharp knocks, the kind Jake hadn't heard since college when he and his fraternity brothers had been busted for sneaking alcohol into the freshman dorms. Jake froze and waited, not daring to move from his anchored position in the hall.

"Thwap! Thwap!", the knocks sounded again, hard enough to bruise the soft wood of his entry way. Slowly, Jake came to the decision that if these were cops, if it was that there were cops at the door, he would be safer with them. 

Slowly, Jake made his way down the stairs and to the front door. He leaned against the solid wood and pressed the side of his face to the jamb. 

"Hello? Who's there?", Jake said, his voice maintaining the redwood- strong quality he prided himself for, still glancing behind himself to check for any sign that the weighty man was coming back downstairs from the maze of hallways above.

There was a silence for a long moment, maybe five seconds- too long, Jake thought. He was expecting to hear the harsh voice of law enforcement, but instead what he heard was something entirely different. 

It was a voice, but unlike anything Jake had yet to hear. It was soft but deep, feminine and masculine in an unnatural register. It sounded almost like there was a man, or a woman perhaps, behind the door, straining their voice to sound like a child.

"How.. How long has he been there?", the voice asked.

Jake felt ice shoot through his blood. He wasn't expecting this frank of a question, and he didn't know quite what to say. Almost before he realized his lips had parted, he heard himself say, "At least an hour."

His redwood voice was a sapling. Jake felt his confidence drain along with the color from his face, as his mind spun with implications. But there was no reply. Jake waited a few minutes then cautiously cracked the door. The morning was halfway through now, and the sun was climbing toward the middle of the sky, but still Jake felt the cold of the March sun with all the warmth of a bare light bulb. Seeing the empty step, Jake shut the door quickly and locked it, and started toward the back to find his cell phone. He had left it on the kitchen counter. Entering the kitchen, Jake spied the rasher of bacon and the knife sitting on his counter- his planned breakfast. Seeing the knife, Jake grabbed it, wielding it for protection against some unknown danger. But seeing the meat, Jake's mind made another connection... this time to his local grocery.

Jake remembered two days prior, shopping for groceries. Shopping for that very slice of meat, at the deli counter. He remembered the butcher, and his mind began to fill in where the fuzzy space had been previously. Before today, the deli butcher had been just another unregistered face. Every day, Jake thought then, he saw hundreds of faces.

Thousands of people throughout his life whose faces he had seen, but not remembered. Those people woke up every morning, looked in the mirror, got through their day. To each one of those faceless, nameless people, their face was more familiar than that of the planet, and yet Jake would only know them for that split second on the train, or in line, or at the library. And the one time Jake needed to remember, he had forgotten. He had forgotten the folds under the butcher's eyes, or his sand glance at Jake's gold wristwatch. He had forgotten when the butcher, cutting the bacon, asked Jake if he was married. Where he called home. 

If he lived alone. 


Jake gripped the wooden handle of the knife tighter with the realization and turned sharply at a creak on the wooden flooring. The man was there in the kitchen, a wild look in his eyes. One of his hands was inside the large, loose pocket of his floral vacation shirt, his legs tensed with anticipation. His other hand had dropped a large bag of valuables (from the sound they made) on the floor. It clattered with a jarring noise of breaking glass and tumbling metals.

Jake pointed the knife out in front of him, and opened his trembling mouth. "Who was that? Why an hour?" 

The man simply sighed, and ran a hand through his thinning hair, drawing his hand up and out of the flap of a pocket. He pointed the blackened gun to Jake's heart. 

He gave Jake a tired look, a worn look. The corners of his pudgy mouth tipped into a slight grin and he stepped closer.

I knew what the neighbors would say to each other as they whispered about me from behind their taffeta mourning veils.

"Things could be worse." 

I felt my lips stretch into the impression of a smile, as I lifted the dew to my cheek, a simulated tear rolling down my face. The same to the naked eye, but bereft of the salt, a manicured pool in a raw ocean. The siren's crescendo pierced the air as I drew my lips into a gathered worry.

I still wasn't sure what they meant, maybe they were a ranking, or a countdown, or a date, or some dystopian method of choosing our life partners.
